headline: ASX surges 1.6% to all-time highs as inflation eases and Iran launches surprise attack on US forces in the Middle East — oil spikes 3.6%.

movers.name: Pilbara Minerals
movers.note: PLS bounced +1.5% today, its best session in a while. Lithium sentiment has been improving as peer IGO reported higher lithium pricing and stronger cash flow, and analysts are keeping a closer eye on earnings trends across the sector. Still down nearly 40% from your entry price — the long-term case rests on a lithium price recovery that hasn't fully arrived yet.

movers.name: Vanguard Diversified High Growth ETF
movers.note: VDHG nudged up +0.44% today, riding the broad ASX rally. As a diversified high-growth ETF it tracks the overall market closely, so today's strong session lifted it along with almost everything else.

movers.name: Vanguard US Total Market ETF
movers.note: VTS edged up +0.39% today. This ETF tracks the entire US share market and is priced in AUD, so it got a slight boost from the broad positive sentiment flowing through global markets. The Aussie dollar dipped slightly today, which also provides a small tailwind for US-denominated assets.

movers.name: Global X Artificial Intelligence ETF
movers.note: GXAI slipped -0.6% today, weighed down by lingering nerves around Google's recent earnings result which triggered a sell-off in AI-exposed tech stocks. Amazon, Meta and Microsoft all report earnings this week (US time), so there's still uncertainty about whether the AI spending story will hold up. Down 21% from your entry — painful, but this is a long-term theme play.

movers.name: Vanguard FTSE Emerging Markets ETF
movers.note: VGE dipped -0.34% today. Emerging markets are being squeezed by two things: the Aussie dollar softening slightly (mixed effect), and Middle East tensions flaring up again with Iran's attack on US forces, which rattles risk appetite for developing-market assets. Nothing structurally broken here.

movers.name: Alphabet Inc. (Google)
movers.note: No live price available yet — US markets open tonight. Last session's close was USD $326.57. Google is in focus after its Q2 earnings sparked a sell-off, with investors worried the company is spending big on AI infrastructure without a clear near-term payoff. Amazon, Meta and Microsoft report this week, which could shift sentiment further.

movers.name: Microsoft
movers.note: No live price yet — Microsoft reports its Q2 earnings tonight (US time). Last close was USD $389.10. Analysts expect a 7% swing either way. Three big AI questions are front of mind: How fast is Azure cloud growing? Is Copilot (Microsoft's AI assistant) generating real revenue? And is the spending on AI data centres paying off? This is one to watch closely tonight.

movers.name: Take-Two Interactive
movers.note: No live price yet — US markets open tonight. Last close was USD $243.95. No specific news today for Take-Two; the stock continues to await its next major catalyst, which remains the GTA VI release timeline.

watch_today.title: MSFT earnings drop tonight — could swing 7% either way
watch_today.detail: Microsoft reports its Q2 results tonight (US time, after 11:30 PM AEST). Analysts say the stock could move 7% in either direction depending on Azure cloud growth numbers and whether AI tools like Copilot are showing real revenue. This is a major event for your MSFT holding. Three questions to watch: Is Azure growth accelerating? Are AI products generating meaningful new revenue? And is the massive AI data centre spending going to pay off? Hold heading into the print — but keep an eye on the result overnight.

watch_today.title: Oil spikes 3.6% on Iran-US clash — watch energy inflation
watch_today.detail: Iran launched what the US military called an 'attempted surprise attack' on American forces in the Middle East overnight. The US and Saudi Arabia struck back with counter-attacks on militias in Iraq. Crude oil (WTI) jumped from $79.26 to $82.10 — a 3.6% jump in one session. This is the kind of event that can push petrol prices higher in Australia within weeks and could keep inflation sticky. Watch this closely.

watch_today.title: Google earnings fallout — AI spending fears drag GXAI down
watch_today.detail: Google's Q2 result last week spooked markets because the company is spending heavily on AI infrastructure but investors couldn't see enough revenue payoff. That sentiment has been dragging AI-exposed ETFs like your GXAI.AX lower (-0.6% today, down 21% from entry). Amazon and Meta also report earnings this week US time, so there's more risk in either direction for AI-themed holdings. Long-term story is intact — sit tight.

watch_today.title: PLS bounces +1.5% — lithium sector showing early signs of life
watch_today.detail: Pilbara Minerals had a solid session today (+1.5%), with peer lithium companies like IGO reporting higher lithium pricing and improved cash flow outlooks. Analysts are watching PLS earnings trends closely. Still down nearly 40% from your entry, so this is a long way from recovery — but the direction is encouraging. Hold and watch for further sector momentum.

watch_today.title: Aussie inflation eases to 3.8% — rate rise fears fade
watch_today.detail: Today's CPI (inflation) data showed Australia's annual inflation rate fell to 3.8%, below expectations. This is good news for mortgage holders — traders have now largely scrapped bets on another RBA interest rate rise. Lower rates are a tailwind for growth assets like your ETFs. Your VDHG, VTS, and VGE holdings all benefit from this kind of environment over time.

watch_today.title: ASX 200 hits 9,038 — broad market strength lifts your ETFs
watch_today.detail: The ASX 200 surged 1.63% today to close at 9,038, a strong session driven by the good inflation data and easing rate-rise fears. Your ASX-listed ETFs (VDHG, VTS, VGE) all participated. Nothing to action here — just a good day for the portfolio's ASX side.

world.summary: The big global stories today centre on a dramatic military flare-up between Iran and US forces in the Middle East, Trump's push to restrict mail-in voting reaching the Supreme Court, and growing concerns about Middle East conflict disrupting global shipping and fuel supplies.

stories.title: Iran launches surprise attack on US forces — US and Saudi Arabia strike back
stories.why_it_matters: Iran launched what the US military described as an 'attempted surprise attack' on American forces in the Middle East in the early hours of Wednesday morning. The US, with Saudi Arabia's support, responded with strikes on Iranian-backed militias in Iraq. Despite the escalation, President Trump said the US and Iran are currently having 'good talks', suggesting both sides are trying to manage the situation. For Australians, the immediate impact is at the petrol pump — crude oil jumped 3.6% to $82.10 a barrel, and if the conflict drags on, that flows through to higher fuel costs within weeks.

stories.title: Middle East tensions slash Red Sea shipping by another 50%
stories.why_it_matters: Red Sea shipping crossings have dropped by a further 50% as conflict in the region spreads, according to new data. The Red Sea is one of the world's most critical shipping routes — it connects Europe and Asia through the Suez Canal. When ships can't use it safely, they reroute around Africa, adding weeks to delivery times and significant cost. This disruption is already feeding into higher prices for imported goods globally, and Australian consumers and businesses that rely on international supply chains will feel it.

stories.title: Trump asks Supreme Court to allow mail-in voting restrictions
stories.source: The New York Times / The Guardian
stories.why_it_matters: The Trump administration has asked the US Supreme Court to greenlight a presidential order restricting mail-in voting — a form of voting used by millions of Americans, particularly older and rural voters. The Justice Department argues the restrictions are needed to prevent fraud. Critics say it's an attempt to suppress votes. This case could reshape how the next US election is run. The Trump administration's attorneys have also been probed for ties to election denial groups, adding to the controversy.

stories.title: US accuses Trump of trying to tilt Brazil's election against Lula
stories.why_it_matters: Brazil's government says the Trump administration is actively working to undermine President Lula da Silva ahead of Brazil's next election — one of the biggest democracies in Latin America. The Wall Street Journal reports Brazil sees a 'Trump-led effort' to tilt the electoral outcome, potentially echoing US interference concerns seen in other countries. Brazil is a major trading partner for Australia, particularly in agriculture and iron ore — so political instability there has real economic ripple effects.

stories.title: Australia weighs first oil refinery in 60 years as treasurer flags Middle East inflation risk
stories.why_it_matters: Australia's Treasurer is warning that the Middle East conflict could push inflation higher through rising fuel costs, and the government is reportedly considering whether to support building Australia's first oil refinery in 60 years to reduce fuel import dependence. Australia currently imports most of its refined fuel — a vulnerability that's been exposed repeatedly by global crises. A local refinery would be a massive infrastructure project and energy security play, though it would take years to build.

markets.summary: The ASX had a cracking session today, surging 1.63% to close at 9,038 — a strong move driven by better-than-expected inflation data easing rate-rise fears. Oil spiked sharply on the Iran-US military clash. Gold also hit new highs. US markets (S&P 500, NASDAQ) haven't opened yet tonight — MSFT earnings after close will be the big one to watch.

indicators.name: ASX 200
indicators.note: Strong session — best move in weeks, driven by easing inflation data and fading rate-rise fears.

indicators.name: S&P 500
indicators.note: Last night's close. US markets open tonight — MSFT earnings are the big event.

indicators.name: NASDAQ
indicators.note: Last night's close. Tech-heavy index will be sensitive to MSFT and Amazon earnings tonight.

indicators.name: Crude Oil (WTI)
indicators.note: Spiked 3.6% on Iran's attack on US forces in the Middle East. Watch for flow-through to Aussie petrol prices.

indicators.name: Gold
indicators.note: Gold hit a new high above $4,100 — investors piling into safe havens amid Middle East tensions.

indicators.name: AUD/USD
indicators.note: The Aussie dollar dipped slightly — investors favouring the USD as a safe haven given the Middle East flare-up.

politics.summary: Big day for Australian economic news — inflation came in lower than expected at 3.8%, effectively killing off bets on another interest rate rise. The RBA governor has been unusually candid about household pressures, and the housing market is cooling more than the RBA anticipated.

stories.title: Inflation drops to 3.8% — rate rise bets scrapped
stories.why_it_matters: Australia's annual inflation rate fell to 3.8% in the latest reading, below what economists were expecting. The Guardian called it 'dodging a bullet' — because if inflation had come in higher, the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) would likely have been forced to raise interest rates again, squeezing mortgage holders even harder. Instead, traders have now largely priced out any further rate rises. This is genuinely good news for anyone with a home loan or variable-rate debt.

stories.title: RBA governor gives unusually candid warning to households
stories.why_it_matters: RBA Governor Michele Bullock issued a notably frank warning to Australian households, acknowledging that cost-of-living pressures remain severe. While the RBA's job is officially just managing inflation, the governor's candid tone signals the bank is acutely aware of the pain households are feeling. Some commentators have described the admission that higher rates were 'part of the plan' as a rare moment of official transparency about the deliberate trade-off between fighting inflation and hurting borrowers.

stories.title: Housing market cooling faster than RBA expected
stories.why_it_matters: The RBA has acknowledged in its latest communications that the housing market has eased 'more than anticipated' — meaning property prices and activity have softened beyond what the bank's own models predicted. This is relevant for homeowners and property investors, as it suggests the RBA's interest rate hikes have bitten harder into the property market than expected. It also gives the RBA more room to consider future rate cuts if conditions continue to weaken.

stories.title: Traders axe RBA rate-rise bets — AFR calls it a turning point
stories.why_it_matters: Following today's inflation data, the AFR reports that financial markets have almost entirely priced out the chance of another RBA rate rise — a significant shift from just weeks ago when many traders expected rates to go higher. The AFR quoted one strategist saying 'everyone has to change their mind.' For long-term investors, this is a meaningful tailwind: lower interest rates over time tend to support share valuations and reduce the cost of borrowing for businesses and households alike.

ai.summary: The big AI story today is a coordinated push from top scientists at OpenAI and Anthropic asking the US government for new tools to manage the pace of AI development — effectively asking for help pumping the brakes. Microsoft also made a bold claim about beating rivals in AI cybersecurity.

stories.title: OpenAI and Anthropic scientists ask US government to help slow AI development
stories.why_it_matters: Senior researchers at OpenAI (the company behind ChatGPT) and Anthropic (maker of Claude) have jointly written to the US government asking for new tools to help manage how fast AI is being developed and deployed. In plain terms: the people building the most powerful AI systems are saying 'we need help slowing this down safely.' They're asking for things like better testing frameworks and oversight mechanisms before powerful new models are released to the public. It's a rare moment of the industry asking for more regulation, not less.

stories.title: OpenAI and Anthropic accused of writing the rulebook their rivals must follow
stories.why_it_matters: There's a conflict-of-interest debate brewing: OpenAI and Anthropic — currently the two most powerful AI companies — appear to be helping design the safety thresholds that any new AI model must meet before it can be released. Critics argue this is like the top two banks writing the rules all banks must follow: it could lock in their advantage and make it harder for newer, smaller AI competitors to launch products. This matters because it could shape who wins the AI race long-term, affecting the value of companies like Google (your GOOG holding) and Microsoft (MSFT).

stories.title: Microsoft claims its new AI beats everyone at cybersecurity
stories.why_it_matters: Microsoft has announced a new AI model it says outperforms OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic specifically in cybersecurity tasks — detecting threats, analysing vulnerabilities, and responding to attacks. This is a significant commercial claim ahead of tonight's MSFT earnings report. Cybersecurity is a huge and growing market, and if Microsoft can dominate AI-powered security, it opens a major new revenue stream. This is a genuine positive for your MSFT holding going into tonight's earnings.

stories.title: Why analysts think Google may be falling behind in the AI race
stories.why_it_matters: Some analysts are asking whether Google has quietly ceded ground in the AI race to OpenAI and Anthropic. Despite being one of the original AI powerhouses, Google's recent earnings disappointed investors who worried its AI spending isn't translating quickly enough into new revenue. The concern is that ChatGPT and Claude are eating into Google Search's dominance — if people use AI assistants instead of Google to answer questions, Google's core advertising business (which funds everything) gets disrupted. This is the central risk for your GOOG holding.

sport.summary: NRL Round 22 kicks off tomorrow night with Cowboys v Roosters. Phil Gould is investigating leaks at the Bulldogs, Panthers legend drops a big retention call, and AFL is heating up ahead of finals with major team news.

stories.title: NRL Round 22: Full team lists confirmed
stories.why_it_matters: Full team lists are out for NRL Round 22. Round opens tomorrow night (Thu 31 Jul) with Cowboys hosting Roosters at Queensland Country Bank Stadium at 7:50 PM. Your local Titans host the Warriors at Cbus Super Stadium on Saturday at 3:00 PM — good chance to head along if you're keen. The Sea Eagles have the bye this week.

stories.title: Gould probes leaks at Bulldogs after 'ugly saga'
stories.why_it_matters: Bulldogs supremo Phil Gould has put two people in his sights after confidential club information was leaked to the media, Nine.com.au reports. Gould described the situation as an 'ugly saga' and is now investigating internally. The Bulldogs have been one of the NRL's most improved clubs under Gould's rebuild — internal leaks could destabilise the culture he's worked hard to build heading into the business end of the season.

stories.title: Panthers legend '90% confident' club will retain its stars
stories.why_it_matters: A Penrith Panthers legend has publicly declared they are '90% confident' the club will hold onto its key players despite significant contract pressure heading into 2027. The Panthers have been the NRL's dynasty team this decade and retaining their core is crucial to sustaining that. No specific names were confirmed in the report, but the comment suggests the club's internal conversations are trending towards keeping the squad together.

stories.title: AFL: Major Bulldogs blow and Dockers' curious ruck call — team tips
stories.why_it_matters: Fox Sports reports a significant injury or selection blow for the Western Bulldogs ahead of a blockbuster AFL fixture, while the Fremantle Dockers have made an unusual call in their ruck selection. With finals approaching, team selection is increasingly critical. The Daicos-Mullin match-up (Nick Daicos of Collingwood vs. a key opponent) is shaping up as the defining individual contest of the round according to The Canberra Times.

stories.title: US Open: Top tennis stars sign up despite boycott fears
stories.why_it_matters: Despite fears of a boycott, a number of top-ranked tennis stars have confirmed their participation in the US Open. The boycott threats had centred around prize money disputes and scheduling concerns. The confirmation of marquee players is good news for the tournament's commercial appeal — and for Australian tennis fans, it means the full field of elite players will be in action at Flushing Meadows.
